case_data.title: Wikibench: Community-Driven Data Curation for AI Evaluation on Wikipedia
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
In 2023 at team at Carnegie Mellon University piloted a new tool that that engaged approximately 17 people in collaborative data curation and system evaluation workshops to review and shape the development of AI content moderation tools on Wikipedia. The project sought to test methods and create re-usable participation that can better enable community-driven AI evaluation.


> AI tools are increasingly deployed in community contexts. However, datasets used to evaluate AI are typically created by developers and annotators outside a given community, which can yield misleading conclusions about AI performance. How might communities be empowered to drive the intentional design and curation of evaluation datasets for AI that impacts them? 
> 
> This was the question explored by the Wikibench project, focussing on Wikipedia, an online community with multiple AI-based content moderation tools currently deployed. The system that enables communities to collaboratively curate AI evaluation datasets, while navigating ambiguities and differences in perspective through discussion. 
> 
> A field study on Wikipedia shows that datasets curated using Wikibench can effectively capture community consensus, disagreement, and uncertainty. Furthermore, study participants used Wikibench to shape the overall data curation process, including refining label definitions, determining data inclusion criteria, and authoring data statements.
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b: The project is currently focused on the English Wikipedia, although the system can be easily extended to other language communities or online platforms.
case_data.headline-findings:
Participant #12: "I was able to explain my rationale on [Wikibench's] talk page. [...] I think that helped to make sure everyone’s view was properly considered."

Participant #11: "I’m quite unsure about my [patrolling] decision sometimes, so it is good to have someone more experienced talk through why they concluded differently from me [...] It’s very enlightening, this [study]."

Participant #8: "[Wikibench] would serve as a good benchmark for different tools, [... and] for whatever models that people come up with afterwards."

Participant #10: "I would say it’s almost like it was built-in [...] It was meant to be there."

Participant #3: "That is the core of decision making on Wikipedia. [...] I think it’s smart that the primary label is not automatically [set as] the majority."

Participant #6: "It’s very useful to have editors with different areas of expertise within Wikipedia working together. [...] In the end, this supports getting better data."

Participant #12: "Wikibench’s feature of showing exactly where different editors align, and that one user cannot force the primary label, helped to facilitate discussions."

Participant #4: "Wikibench provides an avenue for people to calmly discuss stuff because it’s nothing personal."

Participant #1: "I like being able to edit the primary label to help better reflect community consensus. I find the warning helpful as it reminds users that even when being bold, your changes should reflect community consensus, not your personal opinions."
case_data.additional-acknowledgements: Tzu-Sheng Kuo, Aaron Halfaker, Zirui Cheng, Jiwoo Kim, Meng-Hsin Wu, Tongshuang Wu, Kenneth Holstein, Haiyi Zhu
case_data.inclusion-efforts: We collaborate with experienced Wikipedians from the community throughout the project. We also actively reach out to other active Wikipedians and make the recruitment information publicly available on Wikipedia.
case_data.project-title: Wikibench: Community-Driven Data Curation for AI Evaluation on Wikipedia
case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include:
This project should be included in the case book for the following reasons:

(a) The system introduced in the project is specifically designed to reveal potential sources of disagreement regarding the labeling of AI datasets and to facilitate deliberation on these diverse points of view.

(b) The system is intended for communities (Wikipedia editors being an example in this case) who are significantly impacted by the use of AI but historically have not had a say in evaluating the AI systems that greatly impact their knowledge work.

(c) The system represents the first technical infrastructure that enables communities to collectively curate and discuss AI datasets. It also empowers community members with the agency to author label definitions, set data inclusion criteria, and draft data statements to ensure the responsible use of the dataset.

Overall, the project demonstrates the concrete benefits of a collaborative, community-driven approach to AI data curation, rather than leaving it to outsiders.

where-were-participants-from: The project is open to anyone on the English Wikipedia. The actual participants come from around the world, including the United States, Indonesia, Singapore, Germany, Italy, Hungary, Australia, Ireland, and the United Kingdom.
